simple: Money coming in to you: salary, client payments, interest.
example: You get ₹80,000 in your bank on salary day.
depends: Your job, your clients, how many hours you work.
changes: Changes every month if you are a freelancer; fairly steady if salaried.

simple: Money going out: rent, food, bills, shopping.
depends: Where you live and your lifestyle.
changes: Rises when prices rise or when you add EMIs and subscriptions.

simple: What is left after expenses: income minus expenses.
example: ₹80,000 income - ₹60,000 expenses = ₹20,000 saved.
changes: Grows if you earn more or spend less.

simple: The money sitting in your bank account right now.
example: Your bank SMS says 'Avl Bal Rs 45,000'.
changes: Changes after every transaction.

simple: Money leaving your account.
example: 'Rs 500 debited' means you paid ₹500.
changes: Each payment makes your balance smaller.

simple: Money entering your account.
example: 'Rs 50,000 credited' means you received ₹50,000.
changes: Each credit makes your balance bigger.

simple: Instant bank-to-bank payment using a phone app.
example: Paying a chai shop by scanning a QR.
depends: Needs your bank account linked to a UPI app.
changes: Every UPI payment creates an SMS this app can read.

simple: A fixed monthly instalment to repay a loan.
example: A ₹20,000 EMI on a home loan, every month.
depends: Loan amount, interest rate, number of months.
changes: Stays fixed, but part of it is interest and part repays the loan.

simple: The price of money. You earn it on savings and pay it on loans.
example: ₹1,00,000 in a 7% fixed deposit earns about ₹7,000 in a year.
depends: The rate and how long money stays.
changes: Higher rate or longer time means more interest.

simple: Prices rising over time, so the same money buys less.
example: At 6% inflation, ₹100 of goods today costs about ₹201 in 12 years.
changes: Money kept idle slowly loses buying power.

simple: Interest earning interest. This is why starting early matters.
example: ₹10,000 at 10% a year becomes about ₹25,900 in 10 years, without adding anything.
depends: Rate, time, and how long you leave it.
changes: Doubling the time does far more than doubling the amount.

simple: Cash kept aside for surprises like job loss or hospital bills.
example: If you spend ₹30,000 a month, keep ₹90,000 to ₹1,80,000 (3 to 6 months).
depends: Your monthly expenses and job stability.
changes: Grows as your expenses grow. Freelancers need more.

simple: The cash this app asks you never to invest. Set in your Profile.
example: 3 months x ₹35,000 = ₹1,05,000 stays untouched.
depends: Months you choose x monthly expenses.
changes: Raise it if your income is uncertain.

simple: How many months you can live on your balance with no income.
example: ₹2,20,000 balance / ₹35,000 spend = 6.3 months.
changes: Shrinks when you spend more or your balance falls.

simple: How quickly something turns into cash. Bank balance is liquid; a locked-in fund is not.
example: Savings account: instant. PPF: locked for years.
changes: Locking money in tax-savers lowers your liquidity.

simple: A policy that pays hospital bills so one illness does not wipe out your savings.
example: ₹10 lakh cover for about ₹10,000 a year.
depends: Age, city, cover amount, family size.
changes: Premium rises with age and claims.

simple: Pure life cover. If you die during the term, your family gets a lump sum. No payout if you survive.
example: ₹1 crore cover for roughly ₹10,000 a year at 30.
changes: Much cheaper when you buy young.

simple: The tax year: 1 April to 31 March. Not January to December.
example: FY2026-27 runs 1 Apr 2026 to 31 Mar 2027.
changes: Your deadlines and limits reset each 1 April.

simple: The share of your income you pay the government.
example: Higher slabs apply only to the extra income, not all of it.
changes: Changes with your income and the rules each Budget.

simple: Income is taxed in layers. Each layer has its own rate.
example: New regime FY2025-26: nothing up to ₹4L, 5% on the next ₹4L, 10% on the next ₹4L, and so on.
changes: Earning ₹1 more only taxes that ₹1 at the top layer's rate.

simple: Two ways to calculate tax. New has lower rates but few deductions. Old has higher rates but lets you deduct 80C, 80D and more.
example: If your deductions are small, New usually wins. Use the Tax page to check yours.
depends: Your income and how many deductions you can claim.
changes: The better one can flip when your income or investments change.

simple: Income left after allowed deductions. Tax is calculated on this, not on your full income.
example: ₹10L income - ₹1.5L (80C) - ₹50K (standard) = ₹8L taxable (old regime).
changes: More deductions mean lower taxable income.

simple: A fixed amount salaried people subtract automatically.
example: ₹75,000 in the new regime, ₹50,000 in the old.
changes: Set by the Budget. Freelancers do not get it.

simple: An amount the law lets you subtract before tax is calculated.
example: Paying ₹1.5L into PPF reduces taxable income by ₹1.5L (old regime).
depends: The section's limit and your regime.
changes: Each section has a yearly cap you can use up.

simple: A discount that makes tax zero for lower incomes.
example: New regime FY2025-26: no tax if taxable income is up to ₹12 lakh.
changes: Crossing the limit can bring tax back, with some relief just above it.

simple: A 4% extra charge added on top of your tax.
changes: Grows with your tax.

simple: Deduct up to ₹1.5 lakh a year for ELSS, PPF, EPF, life insurance premiums, tuition fees. Old regime only.
example: Put ₹1.5L in ELSS and PPF, and your taxable income drops by ₹1.5L.
depends: Your regime and how much you already used.
changes: Once the ₹1.5L is full, extra adds no further deduction.

simple: A mutual fund that invests in shares and counts under 80C. Locked for 3 years. Value can go up or down.
example: ₹25,000 a month SIP into an ELSS fund.
changes: Returns are not guaranteed and can be negative.

simple: Government-backed long-term savings. PPF is 15 years. EPF is the provident fund cut from salary.
example: ₹20,000 into PPF counts under 80C.
changes: Rates are reviewed by the government every quarter.

simple: A pension account. Up to ₹50,000 extra deduction under 80CCD(1B), old regime.
example: ₹10,000 a month into NPS until you retire.
depends: Chosen mix of shares and bonds.
changes: Money is locked until retirement, with limited early withdrawal.

simple: Deduct health insurance premiums: ₹25,000 (₹50,000 for seniors). Preventive check-ups up to ₹5,000 inside that limit. Old regime only.
example: ₹18,000 premium means ₹18,000 deduction.
changes: Higher if parents are senior citizens.

simple: If you owe ₹10,000 or more after TDS, you pay in four instalments through the year. Mainly freelancers.
example: 15 Jun: 15%, 15 Sep: 45%, 15 Dec: 75%, 15 Mar: 100% (cumulative).
depends: Your estimated tax for the year.
changes: Rises if your income rises. Late payment adds interest.

simple: Tax deducted before you receive money, for example from salary or client payments.
example: Client pays ₹90,000 instead of ₹1,00,000. ₹10,000 went to the tax office on your behalf.
depends: The payer and type of payment.
changes: Counts as tax you already paid.

simple: A pool of many people's money invested in shares or bonds by a professional.
example: ₹500 a month buys a small slice of 50 companies.
depends: The market and the fund's costs.
changes: Value goes up and down. Longer holding lowers the risk of loss.

simple: Investing a fixed amount every month automatically.
example: ₹5,000 on the 5th of every month.
depends: The amount and date you set.
changes: Buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high.

simple: You lock money in a bank for a fixed period at a fixed interest rate. Interest is taxable.
example: ₹1,00,000 for 1 year at 7%.
changes: Rates move with the economy. Breaking early costs a penalty.

simple: How much avoidable tax you may be paying. 100 means nothing left to save.
example: Score 70 means roughly 30% of your tax could be reduced.
changes: Improves as you use more of your limits.

simple: How sure the app is that it labelled a transaction correctly.
example: 95% means a known merchant. Under 50% means please check it.
depends: Whether the merchant was known or a guess.
changes: Improves when you correct a label.

simple: How we measure the app's guesses. Accuracy: how often it is right. Precision: when it says '80C', how often that is true. Recall: of all real 80C payments, how many it found.
example: Precision 96% and recall 90% means 96 of 100 deductions it claims are real, and it finds 90 of 100 real ones.
changes: See the Accuracy page for our real numbers and their limits.
